question: List all 9 vulture species found in India with their scientific names, conservation status, and WPA 1972 schedule.
cardAnswer: Schedule I vultures (all 5): (1) Oriental White-backed Vulture — Gyps bengalensis — Critically Endangered; (2) Slender-billed Vulture — Gyps tenuirostris — Critically Endangered; (3) Long-billed Vulture — Gyps indicus — Critically Endangered; (4) Red-headed Vulture — Sarcogyps calvus — Critically Endangered; (5) Egyptian Vulture — Neophron percnopterus — Endangered (NOT Critically Endangered). question: Describe the complete vulture drug ban situation — primary cause of death, all banned drugs with dates, the Aceclofenac mechanism trap, drugs under surveillance, and safe alternatives.
cardAnswer: The primary cause of vulture death is NSAIDs (Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs) which cause visceral gout and renal (kidney) failure — NOT liver failure. Banned drugs: Diclofenac was banned for veterinary use in 2006 (human formulations continued to be diverted to livestock — the human form was NOT banned). Ketoprofen and Aceclofenac were officially banned by the Ministry of Health in August 2023 for animal use. The Aceclofenac trap: Aceclofenac rapidly metabolises into Diclofenac inside cattle, making it equally lethal even though it appears to be a different drug. Nimesulide has been identified as toxic and is under surveillance with advocacy for a ban (as of 2025). Safe alternatives: Meloxicam and Tolfenamic Acid are both vulture-safe NSAIDs — Meloxicam is not the only safe alternative.

question: Describe the Action Plan for Vulture Conservation 2020–2025, including VSZ definition, rescue centres, the first Pan-India Assessment, Vulture Restaurants, and SAVE/captive breeding status.
cardAnswer: Goal: establish at least one Vulture Safe Zone (VSZ) in every state. A VSZ is defined as a 150 km radius area where no toxic drugs are found in cattle carcasses for two consecutive years. Four new rescue centres were established under this plan at Pinjore, Bhopal, Guwahati, and Hyderabad. The First Pan-India Vulture Assessment (2023–2025) was completed to establish a new population baseline. Vulture Restaurants provide drug-free carcasses near vulture colonies (carcasses are tested before serving); a prominent new restaurant was established in Koderma district, Jharkhand in 2024. SAVE (Saving Asian Vultures from Extinction) is a consortium of BNHS (India) and RSPB (UK). The world's largest vulture conservation breeding centre is the Jatayu Conservation Breeding Centre at Pinjore, Haryana — Asia's first Gyps vulture reintroduction programme started here. As of 2024, captive-bred vultures are being released into West Bengal and Haryana once local VSZs are provisionally identified.

question: Describe the complete conservation framework for the Greater One-Horned Rhino — IRV 2020 status and outcome, its successor, IUCN target, population figures, Kaziranga data, and planned new sites.
cardAnswer: India Rhino Vision (IRV) 2020 officially concluded in April 2021. It met its numerical goal (~3,000 rhinos) but fell short of the distribution goal of spreading rhinos across 7 protected areas — so it did NOT fully achieve all its goals. The successor is the National Rhino Conservation Strategy (2019–Present), which focuses on range expansion and transboundary cooperation with Nepal and Bhutan. A transitional IRV 2.0 bridges the gap. The IUCN SSC target is 4,500 wild rhinos by 2025–2026. Current global population: ~4,075 (late 2025). Assam surpassed 3,000 rhinos (late 2024). Kaziranga holds 2,613 rhinos (2022 Census), accounting for over 70% of the global population. Bihar is planning rhino reintroduction in Valmiki Tiger Reserve (2025–2026).

question: What are the IUCN, WPA, and CITES classifications of the Greater One-Horned Rhino, its Indian range states, and the New Delhi Declaration on Asian Rhinos?
cardAnswer: IUCN status: Vulnerable (since 2008, due to successful recovery — it is NOT Endangered). WPA 1972: Schedule I (highest protection). CITES: Appendix I (bans international trade in horns). question: Describe Project Snow Leopard completely — launch date, administering body, area covered, altitude thresholds, states, population figures, aim, goal, and international listings.
cardAnswer: Project Snow Leopard was launched in January 2009 under MoEFCC. It covers 1.29 lakh sq. km of high-altitude areas, with an altitude threshold of more than 3,000 m in the Western Himalaya and more than 4,000 m in the Eastern Himalaya. States covered: J&K, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, and Arunachal Pradesh (all 5 Himalayan states). Global snow leopard population: ~7,500; India's estimated count: 400–700, representing ~10% of the global population in less than 5% of the global range — meaning India's habitats are high-density areas. Aim: promote a knowledge-based, adaptive conservation framework involving local communities. Goal: safeguard India's high-altitude wildlife heritage through participatory policies and actions. The snow leopard was listed on both CMS (Convention on Migratory Species) and CITES in 2003.
